analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and funds them with higher payroll taxes, including on wages above $400,000.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 105 Democratic cosponsors but never received a committee vote or any floor action in the Republican-controlled House before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits for every beneficiary, use a cost-of-living formula that better matches seniors' spending, and lift the minimum benefit for people who worked many years at low wages. It would pay for this by applying the Social Security payroll tax to all wages above $400,000 and slowly raising the payroll tax rate on all workers and employers over decades. It also would raise the income threshold at which Social Security benefits become taxable.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees, people with disabilities, and survivors would all receive a benefit increase, and the annual cost-of-living adjustment would be recalculated using an index that tracks the higher share of income seniors spend on health care. Lifetime low earners would get a much larger minimum benefit tied to the poverty line. About half of beneficiaries today pay tax on part of their benefits; the bill would spare millions of middle-income retirees from that by raising the thresholds to $50,000 for singles and $100,000 for joint filers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled beneficiaries, and low-wage workers

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the 90% factor in the benefit formula with 93%, raising benefits for every eligible beneficiary beginning in 2016 [S2][S3].
Switches cost-of-living adjustments to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which reflects the higher health-care costs seniors face [S2][S3].
Raises the special minimum benefit for lifetime low earners, scaling up to 125% of the poverty guideline for workers with 30 or more years in the workforce [S2][S3].
Raises the income thresholds at which Social Security benefits become taxable, from $25,000 to $50,000 for single filers and $32,000 to $100,000 for joint filers [S2][S3].
Extends the Social Security payroll tax to all wage income above $400,000, reversing the growing share of earnings that escapes the tax as pay concentrates at the top [S2][S3].
Reallocates payroll tax revenue to the Disability Insurance trust fund, which was facing a funding shortfall [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People earning above $400,000 a year would pay Social Security tax on their full wages, ending the cap's protection of their highest earnings. All workers and employers would see the combined 12.4% payroll tax rise in small steps, reaching 15.3% by 2084. Employers match employee contributions, so businesses with substantial payroll bear half of the rate increase. High earners who newly pay into the system would receive a small credit in their own benefit formula, but far less than they pay in.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners and, gradually, all workers and employers

drawbacks.text: The bill raises payroll taxes on all workers and employers, in increments reaching 7.65% each (15.3% combined, including self-employment) by 2084, a cost that falls on ordinary paychecks even though the heaviest new burden is on high earners [S2][S3].
Applying the tax to wages above $400,000 reaches self-employed professionals and small business owners whose income is reported as self-employment earnings, not just salaried executives [S3].

High earners would receive a small new benefit credit (2% of earnings above $400,000) in return for their additional contributions, a formula concession critics of expanding taxes on high incomes would question [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit increases are broad and immediate, including a meaningful boost for the poorest lifetime earners, while the financing is gradual, front-loading gains for current and near retirees. The main honest objection is that even a slow payroll tax increase is regressive in form, since it applies to wages rather than investment income, though the $400,000 provision concentrates the new burden on the highest earners. On balance, the trade is straightforwardly in favor of beneficiaries, financed mostly by those least dependent on Social Security.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to their Social Security and workforce subcommittees, and it sat there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the Social Security 2100 Act on March 17, 2015 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and the Workforce Committee, with Ways and Means holding primary jurisdiction over Social Security [S1][S5].

In late March and April 2015 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security and the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The bill ended the 114th Congress without a committee vote or floor action, and no roll call was ever taken on it [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with wage income above the $400,000 threshold and their employers were better off because the bill never advanced, since it would have subjected their top earnings to the payroll tax; beneficiaries and low-income seniors, who would have gained larger checks, were worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners whose wages escaped the payroll tax

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 105 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority support within the House Democratic caucus but a minority of the full chamber.

against.name: Paul Ryan
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee with jurisdiction over Social Security never held a markup or vote on the bill; it was referred to subcommittee and went no further.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House agenda in the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: No bill expanding benefits financed by new payroll taxes on high earners was brought to the floor during the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 105 cosponsors were Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority and the Ways and Means chairmanship, the bill never advanced; no Republican cosponsored it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would apply the 12.4% Social Security tax to their full wages, ending the cap that shields their highest earnings. Their gain would be a small benefit-credit concession, far below what they would pay.

industries.industry: Employers, especially those with high-wage payrolls
industries.note: Employers match employee payroll contributions, so both the gradual rate increase and the $400,000 cap change raise their payroll costs. Their cost is the mirror image of the benefit growth ordinary retirees would receive.

industries.industry: Small business owners and self-employed high earners
industries.note: Self-employment income above $400,000 would become subject to the full Social Security tax, reaching professionals and owners who report income this way rather than as wages.
